The Cambrian Period. From five hundred and forty-one to four hundred and eighty-five million years ago, this period marks the beginning of the Paleozoic Era and the Cambrian Explosion—a burst of animal diversification in which most major phyla appeared suddenly in the fossil record. The period gets its name from Cambria, the Latin name for Wales, where the rocks were first studied.

The Cambrian Explosion saw the rapid emergence of arthropods, mollusks, echinoderms, chordates, and other phyla in what geologically amounts to a blink of an eye, a pattern that puzzled Darwin. Trilobites dominated the oceans—armored arthropods with three lobes that would persist for nearly three hundred million years. An even more fearsome creature was Anomalocaris, an apex predator of Cambrian seas that grew up to a metre long, with a circular mouth and grasping appendages.

Most animals lacked hard shells at first. The Burgess Shale fauna in what is now Canada preserves soft-bodied creatures in extraordinary detail, showing us a window into Cambrian life. Oxygen levels rose during the Cambrian, enabling larger bodies and more active metabolisms than earlier life could support. The continents were still scattered, and most life was marine, with the land remaining bare rock and early soil with no plants yet.

This period followed the Proterozoic Eon, during which multicellular life evolved, and preceded the Ordovician Period, when marine life diversified further still.
